988.title: Zhaozhou's tea
988.hook: to every visitor, new or old: go and have some tea
988.tomorrow: The true person of no rank
988.howItsDone: Zen communities may serve tea as part of the day, and the story of Zhaozhou's tea is told in Zen teaching and calligraphy as a reminder to meet the present moment plainly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baizhang's rake, the old teacher who wouldn't eat when his tools were hidden. Your line was no work, no food. What piece of work did you do all the way through? Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

Two monks arrive at a monastery in northern China to see the teacher everyone is talking about. He asks the first one, have you been here before? No, says the monk. Have some tea, says the teacher. He asks the second one the same question. Yes, I've been here before. Have some tea. The temple's manager has been standing nearby, and he can't stand it. Why, he asks, does the one who's new get tea, and the one who's been here get tea too? The teacher calls his name. The manager answers, yes? Have some tea. The teacher was Zhaozhou, and that cup is today's word.
screen: `HAVE YOU BEEN HERE BEFORE?` → `NO. HAVE SOME TEA.` → `YES. HAVE SOME TEA.`

segments.voice: First, the answer that doesn't change. A newcomer and a regular get the same reply. You might expect a teacher's answer to fit the question. Here, Zhaozhou seems to throw the question away. New or old, the cup is the same, and what counts is drinking it. Second, the manager. He is the one who keeps track, who knows who has been here and who hasn't, and he wants the rule explained. Zhaozhou doesn't explain. He calls him by name, and when the man answers, he gets tea too. The one asking for an explanation is offered the same thing as everyone else. Third, the phrase. In Chinese it is three characters, chi cha qu. Readers differ on the last one. Some hear it as go: go and have some tea, off you go. Others hear it as a softer ending: have some tea, then. Either way, it is the plainest thing a host can say, and Zhaozhou says it to everyone. Fourth, why it lasts. Nothing in the story is mysterious. A cup is poured. Someone drinks it. Whatever you thought you needed to understand first can wait until the tea is gone.
screen: `THE SAME ANSWER FOR NEW AND OLD.` · `THE MANAGER WANTS A REASON.` · `CHI CHA QU: GO, HAVE SOME TEA.` · `A CUP POURED, A CUP DRUNK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one cup, fully. If you have a drink near you, tea, coffee, water, hold it in both hands. If not, remember the last cup you held. Feel its warmth or its cool against your palms. Smell it before you sip. Take one sip and let it sit on your tongue before you swallow. Then another. When your mind reaches for the next thing, a message, a plan, come back to the cup. Nothing else to do here. The bell holds the time.
Zhaozhou's tea. The Chan teacher who gave every visitor, new or returning, the same reply: have some tea. Today's word.
Your line: have some tea. Today, drink one cup of tea, or anything, fully, without your phone, as if it were the only thing on the list. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

screen: `DAY 988 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TRUE PERSON OF NO RANK.`

options: explain the teaching behind it

fork.reveal: Zhaozhou called the manager's name, and when he answered, said: have some tea.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite way to change the subject.
what it means: Zhaozhou gives everyone, new, old and the one demanding reasons, the same plain offer to meet this moment.
what a scholar hears: the last character, qu, can be read as go or as a softening particle, and readers have taken it both ways.

989.title: The true person of no rank
989.hook: Linji: a true person of no rank goes in and out of your face
989.howItsDone: Linji's sayings are studied in the Rinzai Zen tradition, which takes its name from him, and the true person of no rank appears among the koans that teachers give students to work on in meditation and interviews.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zhaozhou's tea, the same plain cup for the newcomer, the regular and the man who wanted reasons. Your line was have some tea. Did one cup get your full attention? Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

Name tags at a conference. Doctor, director, intern, guest. Titles on the email signature, ranks on the uniform, the little line under your name on a profile. On any given day a person carries a few of them, and they do real work: they tell people who to ask and what to expect. A Chan teacher named Linji once stood in front of his assembly and pointed at something none of those titles reach. He said it lives right here, in this lump of flesh, and comes and goes through the doors of your face. He gave it a name. Today, Linji.
screen: `DOCTOR. DIRECTOR. INTERN. GUEST.` → `LINJI POINTS PAST THE TITLES.`

segments.voice: First, the sermon. In the Record of Linji, he climbs to the teaching seat and says, roughly: on your lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank, always going in and out through the gates of your face. Those who haven't seen it yet, look, look. Rank here means a place in the order of things: high or low, monk or lay, teacher or student. The true person has none. Second, the challenge. A monk steps forward and asks, what is this true person of no rank? Linji comes down from the seat, grabs him, and says, speak, speak! The monk hesitates, reaching for the right answer. Linji pushes him away with a blunt insult and goes back to his room. Third, why so rough. The monk had turned the true person into a topic, something to be defined. Linji wanted him to show it, right then, in his own seeing and hearing and speaking. The moment he went looking for a correct reply, he had put the rank back on. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. You can be a manager, a parent, a patient, a beginner. Those roles matter, and Linji isn't asking you to throw them away. He is pointing at whatever is looking out of your eyes before any of the labels arrive. It hears the kettle the same way whether you're the boss or the new hire. That one, Linji says, has no rank.
screen: `A TRUE PERSON OF NO RANK.` · `WHAT IS IT? SPEAK, SPEAK!` · `THE MONK REACHES FOR AN ANSWER.` · `BEFORE ANY LABEL ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set one title down. Settle, and breathe. Say silently one label you carry: your job, your role at home, how good or bad you are at something. Feel how it sits on you. Then, for these breaths, put it to one side. Just hear the sounds in the room. Just feel the air at the nostrils. Notice that the hearing and the breathing don't need the title to work. If the label creeps back, that's fine; set it down again. The bell holds the time.
Linji. The Chan teacher who pointed to the true person of no rank, seeing and hearing through your face before any title arrives. Today's word.
Your line: no rank. Today, drop one title for a day. Introduce yourself without it, or do one thing without letting it decide how you act. Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

options: give a careful definition

original.note: Chinese wu wei zhen ren: true person with no rank, no position.

what it means: Linji points at the one who sees and hears through your face before any title, and demands you show it, not define it.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear in zhen ren, true person, an echo of the Daoist realized sage, turned by Linji toward the ordinary person in front of him.

sources.ref: Record of Linji (Linji lu), the 'true person of no rank' sermon

990.title: Cold Mountain
990.hook: Hanshan, the hermit poet of the cliffs
990.howItsDone: Hanshan's poems are read in Chan and Zen circles across East Asia, and Hanshan and Shide appear together in Zen paintings as laughing, carefree figures.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Linji's true person of no rank, going in and out through the face. Your line was no rank. Which title did you set down, and what was left? Day nine hundred ninety.

Poems scratched on rocks. Poems brushed on tree trunks, on the walls of farmhouses, on cliff faces where nobody would think to look. That's how the story goes. A man with a birch-bark hat and worn-out shoes, living in a cave in the mountains, laughing to himself on the paths, now and then wandering down to a monastery kitchen for leftovers. Nobody knew his real name. People called him after the place he lived, and the place gave its name to the poems. In Chinese, Hanshan. In English, Cold Mountain.
screen: `POEMS ON ROCKS AND TREES.` → `A HERMIT IN A CAVE.` → `NAMED FOR HIS MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the man, as tradition tells it. A preface attached to the poems says Hanshan lived among the cliffs in the Tiantai mountains, the same range where Zhiyi had taught, and that he had a friend named Shide who worked in the kitchen of a nearby temple. Shide saved scraps for him. The two of them were taken for madmen by the monks, and loved by later readers as a pair of laughing sages. Some readers doubt how much of the preface to trust, or whether one person wrote every poem. The poems survive either way. Second, the poems. They are plain. Clouds, pines, a stream, the cold. In one, people ask him the way to Cold Mountain, and he answers that no road reaches it; even in summer the ice doesn't melt. In another, he says his mind is like the autumn moon shining in a clear green pool, and nothing compares to it, so how could he explain? Third, the double meaning. Cold Mountain is a real place, rock and wind. It is also, in the poems, a state of mind: clear, quiet, hard to get to by the usual roads. When he says no road reaches it, he means both. Fourth, why he's in this block of teachers. Hanshan never ran a monastery or wrote a commentary. He wrote short poems and left them outside. Some teachers teach from a seat. This one taught from a rock face.
screen: `A HERMIT AND HIS FRIEND SHIDE.` · `NO ROAD REACHES COLD MOUNTAIN.` · `A PLACE, AND A STATE OF MIND.` · `TEACHING FROM A ROCK FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a mountain in the mind. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind a high, quiet place, real or remembered: a hill, a rooftop, a stretch of empty beach. Feel the air there, a little cold, very clear. Let the noise of the day sit down below, out of reach, like a town seen from the cliffs. You don't have to climb anywhere. Just rest where the air is clear, and if a thought comes, let it blow past like wind across the rock. The bell holds the time.
Cold Mountain. Hanshan, the hermit poet of the cliffs, and the clear, hard-to-reach place his poems point to. Today's word.
Your line: no road reaches it. Today, read one short poem outside, any poem, standing in the open air, and let it be the only thing you read for a minute. Day nine hundred ninety.

991.title: Yunmen's one word
991.hook: the master remembered for answering in one word
991.howItsDone: Yunmen's replies appear in koan collections such as the Blue Cliff Record and the Gateless Gate, which Zen students work with in meditation and in private meetings with a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hanshan, the hermit who wrote his poems on rocks. Your line was no road reaches it. Did you read a poem in the open air? Day nine hundred ninety-one.

A monk has been saving up a question. It is big, the kind you ask a great teacher once. He bows, and asks: what is the teaching that goes beyond all the Buddhas and all the ancestors? The hall goes quiet. The teacher, Yunmen, answers with one word. Cake. Not a parable, not a sermon. A sesame cake, an everyday snack. Yunmen was a Chan teacher in southern China, and his students remembered him for answers like that: so short they stop you in the doorway. Today, Yunmen.
screen: `A BIG QUESTION, SAVED UP.` → `BEYOND ALL THE BUDDHAS?` → `CAKE.`

segments.voice: First, the collections. Yunmen's replies were gathered by his students and later set into the koan collections, among them the Blue Cliff Record, where the cake exchange appears. Some readers speak of his one-word barriers: a single word, set across the path like a gate you have to pass through, not walk around. Second, another one. In the Gateless Gate, a monk asks him, what is Buddha? And Yunmen answers with the name of a dried stick, the plain kind once kept in the outhouse. It sounds rude. It is meant to. The monk was holding Buddha up high and far away, and Yunmen dropped it right into the most ordinary corner of the house. Third, what the one word does. A long answer gives the mind something to chew on, and the chewing can go on forever. One word gives it nowhere to go. Cake. The question that seemed so grand meets a small, real thing you could buy and eat today. Teachers say the point is not the cake. The point is what happens in the listener the instant the long thinking stops. Fourth, the cost. One word is easy to say and hard to mean. Yunmen's answers came from long practice, and his students took them away to sit with, sometimes for a long time. Short, here, is not the same as quick.
screen: `ONE-WORD BARRIERS.` · `WHAT IS BUDDHA? A DRIED STICK.` · `ONE WORD GIVES THE MIND NOWHERE TO GO.` · `SHORT IS NOT THE SAME AS QUICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one word for this moment. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself quietly, what is here right now? Don't answer with a sentence. Let one word come. Warm. Tired. Traffic. Breath. Whatever it is, let it be enough. Breathe with that one word for a little while. When the explaining starts up, the because and the but, let it fall away and come back to the single word. If a new word arrives, let it replace the old one. The bell holds the time.
Yunmen. The Chan teacher whose short replies, cake, a dried stick, cut his students' long questions short. Today's word.
Your line: one word. Today, answer one question in one word, honestly, and notice what the silence after it does. Day nine hundred ninety-one.

992.title: Honen
992.hook: the Japanese monk who taught the nembutsu, calling Amida's name, for everyone
992.howItsDone: Followers of Jodo Shu, the Pure Land school that traces itself to Honen, recite Namu Amida Butsu at home and in temple services, sometimes counting recitations on prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yunmen, who answered the grandest question with cake. Your line was one word. What question did you answer in a single word? Day nine hundred ninety-two.

A fisherman can't stop fishing to sit in meditation. A farmer can't memorize the sutras between harvests. A mother with small children has no hours to spend in a temple hall. A monk on a Japanese mountain, a careful and learned scholar, kept asking what the Buddha's teaching could offer people like them. And, his life stories say, he asked it about himself too, because he felt he could not keep the hard practices perfectly either. The answer he found was so short that anyone could carry it: a name, said with trust. The monk was Honen.
screen: `THE FISHERMAN, THE FARMER, THE MOTHER.` → `WHAT IS LEFT FOR THEM?` → `A NAME, SAID WITH TRUST.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha he turned to. The Pure Land sutras tell of a Buddha named Amitabha, Amida in Japanese, who long ago vowed to bring into his Pure Land any being who calls on him with trust. One of those sutras explains the name: his light is immeasurable, shining without obstruction everywhere. Second, the turning point. Honen had studied for years on Mount Hiei, a great center of learning. Tradition says that reading a commentary by the Chinese teacher Shandao, he came on a line about holding Amida's name in mind single-heartedly, walking, standing, sitting or lying down, and he understood that this was the practice Amida's vow itself had chosen. Not one practice among many to be added on. The one. Third, the words. The nembutsu, in Japanese, is Namu Amida Butsu: I take refuge in Amida Buddha. Honen taught that saying it with trust is enough, and that it is open to everyone, learned or not, monk or lay, man or woman, good or struggling. Near the end of his life he wrote a short statement for his students, and it says, in essence: no need for deep learning; just say the name. Fourth, what it cost. His teaching drew strong opposition from older schools, and for a time he was sent into exile. The community that grew from him, the Pure Land school, Jodo Shu, still keeps the name at its heart.
screen: `AMIDA: IMMEASURABLE LIGHT.` · `A LINE IN SHANDAO'S COMMENTARY.` · `NAMU AMIDA BUTSU, FOR EVERYONE.` · `OPPOSITION, AND EXILE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one simple line, said with trust. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can say one short prayer you already know, slowly, letting each word land. If you walk the Pure Land path, that may be Namu Amida Butsu. If you don't pray, choose a plain phrase you trust, the name of someone who loves you, or simply the word thank you, and let it ride the out-breath. No need to understand it all. Just the words, and the breath, again and again. The bell holds the time.
Honen. The Japanese monk who taught that calling Amida's name with trust, the nembutsu, is open to everyone. Today's word.
Your line: just the name. Today, when something feels too complicated to fix, say one simple line you trust, once, and let it be enough for that moment. Day nine hundred ninety-two.

993.title: Shinran
993.hook: Honen's student: even good people are saved, so how much more the bad (Tannisho 3)
993.howItsDone: In Jodo Shinshu, the school that grew from Shinran's teaching, people say Namu Amida Butsu as an expression of gratitude rather than as a practice to earn birth, and the Tannisho is read and discussed in study groups.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Honen, who taught that calling Amida's name with trust is open to everyone. Your line was just the name. What simple line did you let be enough? Day nine hundred ninety-three.

Here is a sentence that sounds like a typo. Even a good person is born in the Pure Land. How much more, then, the bad person. Read it again; it isn't backward by accident. The ordinary saying ran the other way: even a bad person can be saved, so surely a good one will be. The man who flipped it was Honen's student, a monk named Shinran, and his words were remembered and written down by a disciple in a small book called the Tannisho. It is in the third section. Today, Shinran.
screen: `EVEN THE GOOD ARE BORN THERE.` → `HOW MUCH MORE THE BAD.` → `THE TANNISHO, SECTION THREE.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Its title speaks of lamenting differences. A disciple, traditionally named Yuien, wrote down sayings he had heard from Shinran, because after the teacher's death he saw the teaching being bent. So these are remembered words, gathered with care. Second, the flip. In the third section, Shinran explains. A good person, someone confident in their own good deeds, is still leaning partly on their own effort. They haven't wholly entrusted themselves to Amida's vow. They can still be born in the Pure Land, he says, if they turn and entrust. Third, who the vow is for. People full of passions and confusion, he says, cannot free themselves by any practice at all. Amida made the vow out of compassion for exactly them. So the person who knows they are bad, and has nothing left to lean on but the vow, is the one it was meant for in the first place. Not an exception. The point. Fourth, what it is not. This is not permission to do harm. Elsewhere in the same book Shinran warns against taking poison just because there is an antidote. His teaching is about where trust rests: not in how good you've managed to be, but in Amida's compassion, which Pure Land Buddhists call Other Power. The one who can't pretend to be good, in Shinran's eyes, is closest to the door.
screen: `REMEMBERED WORDS, WRITTEN DOWN.` · `THE GOOD STILL LEAN ON THEMSELVES.` · `THE VOW WAS MADE FOR THE BAD.` · `NOT PERMISSION: AN ANTIDOTE, NOT POISON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look kindly at someone flawed. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a person whose faults you know well. Someone who irritates you, or lets people down. Maybe it's you. Don't excuse what they do, and don't argue the case. Just notice that they are struggling, as people do. On each out-breath, let a little of the judging loosen, the way you'd loosen a too-tight grip. If it's hard, come back to the breath and try again with something smaller. The bell holds the time.
Shinran. Honen's student, who taught that Amida's vow was made above all for those who know they can't save themselves. Today's word.
Your line: how much more the bad. Today, be kind to one flawed person, in a small way they may not even notice. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

994.title: Shinran's family
994.hook: Shinran married and raised a family, neither monk nor layman
994.howItsDone: In Jodo Shinshu, priests may marry, and a local temple may be run by a family who lives on its grounds and serves the community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shinran's sentence that sounds backward: even the good are born in the Pure Land, so how much more the bad. Your line was how much more the bad. Who did you manage to be kind to? Day nine hundred ninety-four.

A box of old letters, kept in a temple archive for a very long time, then read again. They are from a mother to her grown daughter. She writes about the man she married, how she first understood who he was, what she remembered of his hard years. The man was Shinran. The woman was his wife, Eshinni. A Buddhist monk with a wife, children, a household and letters home was not the usual picture in his world. Shinran found his own phrase for what he had become: neither monk nor layman. Today, Shinran's family.
screen: `A MOTHER'S LETTERS TO HER DAUGHTER.` → `SHINRAN AND ESHINNI.` → `NEITHER MONK NOR LAYMAN.`

segments.voice: First, how it happened. When the authorities moved against Honen's community, Shinran was among those sent into exile, and he was stripped of his status as a monk. He never went back to the monastery life. With his wife, Eshinni, he raised children, and lived among farmers and ordinary people in the provinces, teaching the nembutsu to whoever came. Second, his phrase. In the closing pages of his major work, the Kyogyoshinsho, he writes of himself that he is therefore neither monk nor layman. He took the name Gutoku, which carries the sense of a foolish, stubble-haired one: no longer a shaved monk, not quite a layman either. Third, the letters. Eshinni's letters to their daughter, Kakushinni, are among the ways we see Shinran as a person and not only as a teacher. They show a wife who respected him deeply and a family that lived through hard times together. Fourth, why it matters. Shinran's teaching put all the weight on Amida's vow, not on how pure a life a person could manage. A married man, raising children, working out the next meal, needed the vow as much as anyone, and could receive it as fully. In Jodo Shinshu, the school that grew from his teaching, temple priests may marry and raise families, and a temple can also be a family's home. Ordinary life, in this telling, is not a step down from the path. It is where the path is walked.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one ordinary thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the most everyday part of your life: the dishes, the commute, the laundry, the people you live with or call. Choose one. Hold it in mind without wishing it were something grander. Notice the care that is already in it, yours or someone else's. Let one breath be a quiet thank you to it. Then another. The bell holds the time.
Shinran's family. The teacher who married Eshinni, raised children, and called himself neither monk nor layman. Today's word.
Your line: neither monk nor lay. Today, give one plain family moment, a shared meal, a phone call, a goodnight, your full attention, as if it were part of the path. Day nine hundred ninety-four.

fork.setup: you're Shinran. you've been exiled and stripped of your status as a monk. what do you do next?
options: fight to be restored to the monastery
marry, raise a family, and keep teaching
stop teaching altogether
fork.reveal: Shinran married, raised children, lived among ordinary people, and kept teaching the nembutsu, neither monk nor layman.

original.note: Japanese hiso hizoku: neither monk nor layman, Shinran's phrase for himself.
